title: India stays Asia’s third power as gap with China narrows to its smallest since 2018, Lowy index finds
dek: The 2026 Asia Power Index credits India’s defence ties and BrahMos sales in South-East Asia, but marks down its economy and says its low profile in the Gulf conflict hurt its standing.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
India has kept its place as the third most powerful country in Asia, and the gap between it and China is now the narrowest since the Lowy Institute began measuring it in 2018, according to the Sydney-based think tank's 2026 Asia Power Index, published this week.

India's overall score rose by 0.5 points to 40.5 out of 100, behind the United States and China, and it remains the only country the index classes as a "major power" below those two. But the distance to Beijing is still wide: China's measured power is about 80% greater than India's, the institute's analysts wrote, according to reports.

## What the index found

The index ranks 27 countries and territories on 131 indicators grouped into eight measures, from economic and military capability to diplomatic and cultural influence. "While its economy and diplomacy showed mixed results in 2026, India grew more influential in Asia," the report said, according to reports.

India's gains came mostly from its links with other countries. Its defence networks improved, which the institute put down to greater regional defence engagement and sales of BrahMos missiles to South-East Asia, though India still ranks only ninth on that measure, with 18.6 points. It moved up two places to seventh for economic relationships, and the institute noted that India was one of the few countries whose economic ties did not weaken this year. Its score for future resources, a projection of economic, demographic and military capacity, rose to 56.2, ranked third, and cultural influence rose to 43.8.

Diplomatic influence, at 70.3 points, held up. In the index's survey of experts, Prime Minister Narendra Modi rose three places to be rated the second most effective leader in the region, after China's Xi Jinping. The institute added, however, that India's low profile during the Gulf conflict weighed on views of Mr Modi's global leadership.

India's economic capability score fell to 26.4, although it kept third place on that measure. The institute linked the fall partly to a weaker rupee, changes to the IMF's methods of measuring economies and a drop of nearly $20 billion in India's outbound investment, according to reports.

## What it means for India

The index is a research product, not an official ranking, but it is widely cited in Asian capitals, and its findings track the main lines of India's foreign policy this year. The gains in defence networks and economic relationships reflect New Delhi's push to sell arms and build ties in South-East Asia, where China is ASEAN's largest trading partner and a rival claimant to several members in the South China Sea.

The persistent weakness is economic. India's lower economic capability score and its smaller outbound investment matter because China's influence across India's neighbourhood, from ports and power plants in Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Myanmar to loans in Nepal, rests on money India has struggled to match. A narrower overall gap does not change the fact that China's economy and military remain several times larger.

The finding on the Gulf conflict is a reminder that the index rewards visible regional leadership as well as capacity. India has avoided taking sides in the US-Iran confrontation, which has disrupted its oil and gas imports through the Strait of Hormuz.

## What happens next

The Lowy Institute publishes the index once a year. The Declaration found no official comment from New Delhi on the 2026 findings. India's ranking was also third in the 2025 edition, which first placed it in the major-power tier.
